newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. begins debate Tuesday on Israel building plan.
newsitem.headline: U.N. begins debate Tuesday on Israel building plan.

text.p: The Security Council will begin a debate on Tuesday on Israel's recent decision to build a new Jewish neighbourhood in East Jerusalem, the council president said.

Speaking to reporters on Monday after closed-door consultations, ambassador Zbigniew Wlosowicz of Poland said: "The members of the Security Council...decided that tomorrow, at 1030 am (1530 gmt), we will have a formal meeting on occupied territories."

The meeting was requested by the Arab group of states after Israel decided last Wednesday to build 6,500 homes for Jews on a tree-covered hill between Jerusalem and Bethlehem, called Har Homa by Israel and Jabal Abu Ghneim by the Palestinians. Israel captured the hill during the 1967 Middle East war.
Council members said they expected a large number of speakers, including non-members of the council, to take part in the debate, which was likely to continue at least through Wednesday.
The Palestine Liberation Organisation's U.N. observer, Nasser al-Kidwa, told reporters he doubted that President Yasser Arafat would take part in the debate.

Arafat, who conferred with President Bill Clinton in Washington on Monday, was due in New York late on Tuesday for a one-day visit. He is to confer with Secretary-General Kofi Annan on Wednesday and hold a number of other meetings before leaving later that day for Houston, Texas, to met former President George Bush and former Secretary of State James Baker.
But a council source said Arafat was expected to meet informally with council members some time on Wednesday.
Al-Kidwa, who said last week Arab states would submit a resolution to the Security Council, said European members were now working on a text. He did not specify which countries were involved.
The five European members of the 15-nation council are: Britain, France, Portugal, Sweden and Russia.
"We think that to have a European text in principle is significant politically. So definitely we will give it priority, if at all possible. We need to take a look at the text," al-Kidwa said.

The 54-member Islamic group of states issued a statement after a closed-door meeting on Monday expressing deep concern over "illegal measures by Israel, inter alia, the building of settlements in the occupied Palestinian territories, including Jerusalem, and the occupied Syrian Golan."

"The Israeli decision on February 26, 1997 to build a new settlement in East Jerusalem in Jabal abu Ghneim constitutes the latest attempt by Israel at pre-empting the outcome of negotiations on final status by changing the legal status and demographic composition of Jerusalem."
This was a reference to talks due to begin soon between Israel and the Palestinians on a number of the most thorny issues still to be resolved, including the question of Jerusalem.
Israel has vowed that the city will remain its undivided capital while the Palestinians want East Jerusalem to be the capital of a Palestinian state.

The Islamic group's statement called on "the international community, including the Security Council, to take urgent steps to ensure that the government of Israel reverses its decision and renounce any settlement activity."
